title: A star circles our galaxy’s black hole every 16 years, at up to 7,650 km/s

cover.alt: Animation of glowing stars on looping blue orbit lines around a small marked point, the black hole at the centre of the Milky Way.

body: **S2** is a star of about 14 solar masses orbiting Sagittarius A*, the black hole at the centre of the Milky Way. Its orbit is a stretched ellipse: at its closest it passes just 17 light-hours from the black hole, moving at almost 3% of the speed of light. From the size and period of that orbit, astronomers can weigh the invisible object: about 4.3 million Suns. When S2 swept past in May 2018, the change in its light matched the predictions of Einstein’s general relativity.

slides.alt: Animation of stars moving along blue orbit lines around a small circle that marks the black hole; one bright star swoops in close past the circle and swings back out.
slides.caption: An animation by ESO, the European Southern Observatory, of stars orbiting the black hole at the centre of the Milky Way (the small circle). The bright star S2 dives in close, then swings back out.

slides.heading: The star and the black hole it circles
slides.note: Masses; S2’s is an ESO estimate. The black hole is about 300,000 times heavier

slides.question: At its closest, S2 is how many times the Earth–Sun distance from the black hole?
slides.explanation: About 120 times. Light crosses that gap in just 17 hours.

slides.question: What did S2’s close pass in 2018 show?
slides.explanation: S2’s light was stretched to longer wavelengths by the black hole’s gravity and by its speed, just as general relativity predicts.
